'''Stephen Ronald Quake''' (born 1969) is an American physicist, inventor, and entrepreneur, known for developing [[Microfluidics|microfluidic]] large-scale integration and for innovations in [[genomics]] and [[molecular diagnostics]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Clarivate Reveals Citation Laureates 2022 - Annual List of Researchers of Nobel Class |url=https://ir.clarivate.com/news-events/press-releases/news-details/2022/Clarivate-Reveals-Citation-Laureates-2022---Annual-List-of-Researchers-of-Nobel-Class/default.aspx |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=ir.clarivate.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Steve Quake FRS {{!}} Royal Society Fellow |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/stephen-quake-37389/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=royalsociety.org |language=en}}</ref> He pioneered several [[liquid biopsy]] diagnostics, including [[Noninvasive prenatal testing|noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT)]], novel tests for [[Transplant rejection|organ transplant rejection]], infectious disease, and [[cancer]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=H. == Early life and education ==
Quake earned his B.S. in [[physics]] and M.S. in [[mathematics]] from [[Stanford University|Stanford]] in 1991, and his D.Phil. in [[theoretical physics]] from [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]] in 1994 as a [[Marshall Scholarship|Marshall Scholar]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stephen Quake {{!}} Bioengineering |url=https://profiles.stanford.edu/6281 |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=profiles.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Marshall Scholar Alumni by Year from Association of Marshall Scholars |url=https://marshallscholars.org/alumni-by-year |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Association of Marshall Scholars |language=en-US}}</ref> His thesis research was in [[statistical mechanics]] and the topological effects of knots on polymers. He did his postdoctoral work at Stanford in single-molecule [[biophysics]] with [[Steven Chu]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Quake |first1=Stephen R. |last2=Babcock |first2=Hazen |last3=Chu |first3=Steven |date=July 1997 |title=The dynamics of partially extended single molecules of DNA |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/40588 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=388 |issue=6638 |pages=151–154 |doi=10.1038/40588 |pmid=9217154 |bibcode=1997Natur.388..151Q |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Academic career ==
Quake joined the faculty of the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1996 at the age of 26, where he rose through the ranks and was ultimately appointed the Thomas and Doris Everhart Professor of [[Applied physics|Applied Physics]] and [[Physics]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-31 |title=Steve Quake, Biophysicist, Bioengineer, and Biohub Leader |url=http://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews-updates/steve-quake |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Heritage Project |language=en}}</ref> He moved back to [[Stanford University]] in 2005 to help launch a new department in [[Bioengineering]], where he was the Lee Otterson Professor and held appointments in [[Applied physics|Applied Physics]] (and by courtesy, [[Physics]]) through 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Celebrating Twenty-Plus Years of Bioengineering at Stanford {{!}} Bioengineering |url=https://bioengineering.stanford.edu/celebrating-twenty-plus-years-bioengineering-stanford |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=bioengineering.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref> From 2006 to 2016, he was an Investigator of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stephen R. Quake, DPhil {{!}} Former Investigator {{!}} 2006-2016 |url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/stephen-r-quake |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.hhmi.org |language=en}}</ref> He has held honorary faculty positions such as the Andrew D. White Professor-at-Large at [[Cornell University]] and Non-resident Fellow at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies|Salk Institute]], and has been a visiting professor at the [[Collège de France]] and [[ESPCI Paris|ESPCI]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stephen Quake – Andrew D. White Professors-at-Large Program |url=https://adwhiteprofessors.cornell.edu/professors-at-large/stephen-quake/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=adwhiteprofessors.cornell.edu |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Stephen Quake and David Julius named Salk Institute Nonresident Fellows |url=https://www.salk.edu/news-release/stephen-quake-and-david-julius-named-salk-institute-nonresident-fellows/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Salk Institute for Biological Studies |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-14 |title=Stephen Quake {{!}} Collège de France |url=https://www.college-de-france.fr/en/person/stephen-quake |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.college-de-france.fr |language=en}}</ref> In May 2026, Quake was appointed Professor of Biophysics and [[Biomedical engineering|Biomedical Engineering]] in the Department of [[Biological systems engineering|Biosystems]] Science and Engineering (D-BSSE) at [[ETH Zurich]] in Basel, Switzerland.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-22 |title=Eleven professors appointed |url=https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/05/eleven-professors-appointed.html |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=ETH Zurich |language=en}}</ref>

== Research and contributions ==

=== Microfluidics and large-scale integration ===
Quake developed the biological equivalent of the [[integrated circuit]] through the development of microfluidics, also known as a "[[Lab-on-a-chip|lab on a chip]]."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thorsen |first1=Todd |last2=Maerkl |first2=Sebastian J. |last3=Quake |first3=Stephen R. |date=2002-10-18 |title=Microfluidic Large-Scale Integration |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1076996 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=298 |issue=5593 |pages=580–584 |doi=10.1126/science.1076996 |pmid=12351675 |bibcode=2002Sci...298..580T |issn=0036-8075}}</ref> He invented multilayer [[Soft lithography|soft-lithography]] devices, made from [[elastomer]], which have integrated valves and pumps to control fluids.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Unger |first1=Marc A. |last2=Chou |first2=Hou-Pu |last3=Thorsen |first3=Todd |last4=Scherer |first4=Axel |last5=Quake |first5=Stephen R. |date=2000-04-07 |title=Monolithic Microfabricated Valves and Pumps by Multilayer Soft Lithography |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.288.5463.113 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=288 |issue=5463 |pages=113–116 |doi=10.1126/science.288.5463.113 |pmid=10753110 |bibcode=2000Sci...288..113U |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He and colleagues then demonstrated '''microfluidic large-scale integration (mLSI)''', packing thousands of addressable valves onto a single chip to route, mix, meter, and store tiny liquid volumes for complex workflows.<ref name=":4" /> Using these platforms, his lab built high-throughput tools for biophysics and [[structural biology]], including microfluidic methods for [[protein crystallization]] and for measuring [[Transcription factor|transcription-factor]] [[binding energy]] landscapes across many sequences in parallel.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=Carl L. |last2=Skordalakes |first2=Emmanuel |last3=Berger |first3=James M. |last4=Quake |first4=Stephen R. |date=2002-12-24 |title=A robust and scalable microfluidic metering method that allows protein crystal growth by free interface diffusion |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=99 |issue=26 |pages=16531–16536 |doi=10.1073/pnas.262485199 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=139178 |pmid=12486223 |bibcode=2002PNAS...9916531H }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maerkl === Non-Invasive Prenatal Diagnostics (NIPT) ===
A central theme of Quake's genomics work is diagnostics built by counting individual DNA or RNA molecules rather than averaging ensemble signals.<ref name=":5" /> In 2008, his team showed that [[noninvasive prenatal testing]] (NIPT) could detect fetal chromosomal [[Aneuploidy|aneuploidies]] by [[shotgun sequencing]] fragments of [[Cell-free fetal DNA|cell-free DNA]] in maternal blood.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=H. Christina |last2=Blumenfeld |first2=Yair J. |last3=Chitkara |first3=Usha |last4=Hudgins |first4=Louanne |last5=Quake |first5=Stephen R. |date=2008-10-21 |title=Noninvasive diagnosis of fetal aneuploidy by shotgun sequencing DNA from maternal blood |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=105 |issue=42 |pages=16266–16271 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0808319105 |doi-access=free |pmc=2562413 |pmid=18838674}}</ref> In 2012, they reported that the fetal [[genome]] could be inferred from a maternal blood sample, illustrating how [[sequencing]] and [[computation]] can replace invasive procedures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=H. Christina |last2=Gu |first2=Wei |last3=Wang |first3=Jianbin |last4=Blumenfeld |first4=Yair J. |last5=El-Sayed |first5=Yasser Y. |last6=Quake |first6=Stephen R. |date=July 2012 |title=Non-invasive prenatal measurement of the fetal genome |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=487 |issue=7407 |pages=320–324 |doi=10.1038/nature11251 |pmid=22763444 |pmc=3561905 |bibcode=2012Natur.487..320F |issn=1476-4687}}</ref>

=== Cell-free DNA in transplantation ===
The group extended [[cell-free DNA]] analysis to [[Transplantation (medicine)|transplant medicine]], demonstrating that a rise in donor-derived DNA in a recipient's plasma provides a universal, noninvasive signal of [[Transplant rejection|organ rejection]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Snyder |first1=Thomas M. |last2=Khush |first2=Kiran K. |last3=Valantine |first3=Hannah A. |last4=Quake |first4=Stephen R. |date=2011-04-12 |title=Universal noninvasive detection of solid organ transplant rejection |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=108 |issue=15 |pages=6229–6234 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1013924108 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=3076856 |pmid=21444804 |bibcode=2011PNAS..108.6229S }}</ref>

=== Single-cell methods and lineage reconstruction ===
Quake's lab helped benchmark [[Single-cell sequencing|single-cell RNA-sequencing]] methods and used them to map how cells in tissues change during development and disease.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Angela R. |last2=Neff |first2=Norma F. |last3=Kalisky |first3=Tomer |last4=Dalerba |first4=Piero |last5=Treutlein |first5=Barbara |last6=Rothenberg |first6=Michael E. |last7=Mburu |first7=Francis M. |last8=Mantalas |first8=Gary L. |last9=Sim |first9=Sopheak |last10=Clarke |first10=Michael F. |last11=Quake |first11=Stephen R. |date=October 2013 |title=Quantitative assessment of single-cell RNA-sequencing methods |journal=Nature Methods |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=41–46 |doi=10.1038/nmeth.2694 |pmid=24141493 |pmc=4022966 |issn=1548-7105}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Treutlein |first1=Barbara |last2=Brownfield |first2=Doug G. |last3=Wu |first3=Angela R. |last4=Neff |first4=Norma F. |last5=Mantalas |first5=Gary L. |last6=Espinoza |first6=F. Hernan |last7=Desai |first7=Tushar J. |last8=Krasnow |first8=Mark A. |last9=Quake |first9=Stephen R. |date=April 2014 |title=Reconstructing lineage hierarchies of the distal lung epithelium using single-cell RNA-seq |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=509 |issue=7500 |pages=371–375 |doi=10.1038/nature13173 |pmid=24739965 |pmc=4145853 |bibcode=2014Natur.509..371T |issn=1476-4687}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Travaglini |first1=Kyle J. |last2=Nabhan |first2=Ahmad N. |last3=Penland |first3=Lolita |last4=Sinha |first4=Rahul |last5=Gillich |first5=Astrid |last6=Sit |first6=Rene V. |last7=Chang |first7=Stephen |last8=Conley |first8=Stephanie D. |last9=Mori |first9=Yasuo |last10=Seita |first10=Jun |last11=Berry |first11=Gerald J. |last12=Shrager |first12=Joseph B. |last13=Metzger |first13=Ross J. |last14=Kuo |first14=Christin S. |last15=Neff |first15=Norma |date=November 2020 |title=A molecular cell atlas of the human lung from single-cell RNA sequencing |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=587 |issue=7835 |pages=619–625 |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2922-4 |pmid=33208946 |pmc=7704697 |bibcode=2020Natur.587..619T |issn=1476-4687}}</ref> They also showed that single-cell data could reconstruct cellular lineages in mammalian tissues, providing a template for later atlas efforts.<ref name=":6" />

=== Cell atlases and open resources ===
Building on these methods, Quake co-led '''''Tabula Muris''''' and '''''Tabula Sapiens''''', large consortia that profiled hundreds of thousands of cells across mouse and human organs, and released '''open datasets and tools''' that became community reference resources.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

=== AI and computational biology ===
Recent work explores [[machine learning]] and foundation models that learn '''universal representations of cells''' across species, aiming to make cross-tissue and cross-organism comparisons as routine as sequence alignment.<ref>{{Cite bioRxiv |last=Rosen |first=Y. |date=April 2026 |title=Universal Cell Embeddings: A Foundation Model for Cell Biology |biorxiv=10.1101/2023.11.28.568918 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pearce |first1=James D. |last2=Simmonds |first2=Sara E. |last3=Mahmoudabadi |first3=Gita |last4=Krishnan |first4=Lakshmi |last5=Palla |first5=Giovanni |last6=Istrate |first6=Ana-Maria |last7=Tarashansky |first7=Alexander |last8=Nelson |first8=Benjamin |last9=Valenzuela |first9=Omar |last10=Li |first10=Donghui |last11=Quake |first11=Stephen R. |last12=Karaletsos |first12=Theofanis |date=2026-05-07 |title=TranscriptFormer: A generative cell atlas across 1.5 billion years of evolution |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aec8514 |journal=Science |volume=393 |issue=6806 |article-number=eaec8514 |language=en |doi=10.1126/science.aec8514 |pmid=42096520 |bibcode=2026Sci...393c8514P |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Leadership and service ==

=== Founding and building the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub Network (2016–2025) ===
In 2016, Quake co-founded the [[Chan Zuckerberg Biohub]] (San Francisco) as a university–nonprofit collaboration linking [[University of California, San Francisco|UCSF]], [[University of California, Berkeley|UC Berkeley]], and [[Stanford University]], and served as co-president with [[Joseph DeRisi|Joe DeRisi]] to establish investigator programs, internal research groups, and shared technology platforms.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Anwar |first=Yasmin |date=2016-09-21 |title=UC Berkeley to partner in $600M Chan Zuckerberg science 'Biohub' |url=https://news.berkeley.edu/2016/09/21/biohub/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Berkeley News |language=en}}</ref> Quake then served as founding president of the CZ Biohub Network and launched new Biohub institutes in Chicago (with the [[University of Chicago]], [[Northwestern University|Northwestern]], and [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|UIUC]]) and New York ([[Columbia University|Columbia]], [[Rockefeller University|Rockefeller]], [[Yale University|Yale]]).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rouleau |first=Michael |date=2023-03-02 |title=CZI Launches New Biohub in Chicago |url=https://chanzuckerberg.com/newsroom/biohub-chicago-engineer-technologies-measure-human-biology/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Chan Zuckerberg Initiative |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Richmond |first=Jackie |date=2024-10-10 |title=CZI, State and City Leaders Launch Chan Zuckerberg Biohub NY |url=https://chanzuckerberg.com/newsroom/new-york-biohub-launches/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Chan Zuckerberg Initiative |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Head of Science at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (2022–2025) ===
In June 2022, Quake was named Head of Science at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, overseeing grant programs, technology development, and the Biohub network's scientific integration.<ref>{{Cite web |last=chadcampbell |date=2022-06-23 |title=Stephen Quake Named New Head of Science at CZI |url=https://chanzuckerberg.com/newsroom/stephen-quake-named-new-head-of-science-at-the-chan-zuckerberg-initiative/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Chan Zuckerberg Initiative |language=en-US}}</ref> He led CZI's pivot towards AI-enabled biology, launching their internal AI program and building their first [[Graphics processing unit|GPU]] compute cluster.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rouleau |first=Michael |date=2023-09-19 |title=New AI Cluster Will Create Predictive Models of Cells |url=https://chanzuckerberg.com/newsroom/czscience-builds-ai-gpu-cluster-predictive-cell-models/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Chan Zuckerberg Initiative |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== University and community service ===
At [[Stanford University]], Quake helped build and lead the Bioengineering department, where he served a term as co-chair. He held a joint appointment in [[Applied physics|Applied Physics]], served on numerous national committees, and has been a champion of open science. The CZ Biohub was the first institution to require the use of preprints for all of its publications, and at CZI, Quake led the creation and funding of [https://openrxiv.org/introducing-openrxiv/ OpenRxiv], which established [[bioRxiv]] and [[medRxiv]] as an independent non-profit organization.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Teal |first=Tracy |date=2025-03-11 |title=Introducing openRxiv: a new independent home for preprint sharing in the life sciences |url=https://openrxiv.org/introducing-openrxiv/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=openRxiv |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Manager |first=Ingrid Bray, Senior Corporate Brand & Communications |date=2025-03-11 |title=openRxiv launch to sustain and expand preprint sharing in life and health sciences - BMJ Group |url=https://bmjgroup.com/openrxiv-launch-to-sustain-and-expand-preprint-sharing-in-life-and-health-sciences/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=bmjgroup.com |language=en-GB}}</ref> In the non-profit world, Quake currently serves as a trustee of the [[Carnegie Institution for Science]] and is a director of the [https://proteininnovation.org/ Institute for Protein Innovation] and of the [https://www.23andmeresearchinstitute.org/ 23andMe Research Institute].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-19 |title=Board of Trustees |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/about/board-trustees |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=carnegiescience.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gura |first=Trisha |date=2026-03-02 |title=His next big idea might emerge from something small: Stephen Quake joins IPI Board |url=https://proteininnovation.org/2026/03/stephen-quake-joins-ipi-board/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Institute for Protein Innovation |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=23andMe Research Institute Names Brad Margus and Stephen Quake, D.Phil., to Board of Directors |url=https://www.mediacenter.23andme.com/press-releases/23andMe-research-institute-names-brad-margus-and-stephen-quake-to-board-of-directors |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.mediacenter.23andme.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
Quake is one of roughly two dozen people to have been elected to all of the [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine|National Academies]] in the United States, including the [[National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Science]], the [[National Academy of Engineering]], the [[National Academy of Medicine]], and the [[National Academy of Inventors]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-05-02 |title=Quake elected to National Academy of Sciences {{!}} Stanford University School of Engineering |url=https://engineering.stanford.edu/news/quake-elected-national-academy-sciences |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=engineering.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2013 |title=Dr. Stephen R. Quake |url=https://www.nae.edu/CheckRobotPage.html?redirectUrl=/69246/Dr-Stephen-R-Quake |access-date=2026-05-23 |website=www.nae.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-07 |title=Stephen R. Quake, DPhil, MS - NAM |url=https://nam.edu/team/steve-quake/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=nam.edu |language=en-US}}</ref> He has also been elected as a fellow of the [[Royal Society]], the [[American Physical Society]], the [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]], and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Steve Quake FRS {{!}} Royal Society Fellow |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/stephen-quake-37389/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=royalsociety.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Max Delbrück Prize in Biological Physics |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/prize/delbruck-prize |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260428053154/https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/prize/delbruck-prize |archive-date=2026-04-28 |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-23 |title=Stephen R. Quake {{!}} American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/stephen-r-quake |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref>

He received the [[National Institutes of Health Director's Pioneer Award|NIH Director's Pioneer Award]] (2004), the [[Lemelson–MIT Prize]] (2012), the Jacob Heskel Gabbay Award (2015), the [[Max Delbruck Prize|Max Delbrück Prize]] in Biological Physics (2016), the Tel Aviv University International Prize in Biophysics, and the Royal Society of Chemistry's Pioneer of Miniaturization Award (2010).<ref>{{Cite web |title=NIH Director's Pioneer Award Program - 2004 Award Recipients {{!}} NIH Common Fund |url=https://commonfund.nih.gov/pioneer/AwardRecipients04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181010095825/https://commonfund.nih.gov/pioneer/AwardRecipients04 |archive-date=2018-10-10 |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=commonfund.nih.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Stephen Quake {{!}} Lemelson |url=https://lemelson.mit.edu/award-winners/stephen-quake |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=lemelson.mit.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Gabbay Award Winners |url=https://www.brandeis.edu/rosenstiel/gabbay-award/past.html |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.brandeis.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-09-05 |title=Past Laureates of the Tel Aviv University International Prize in Biophysics |url=https://english.tau.ac.il/tau_prize_in_biophysics_past_laureates |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Tel Aviv University |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Michael |title=Stephen Quake wins Pioneers of Miniaturisation Lectureship – Lab on a Chip Blog |url=https://blogs.rsc.org/lc/2010/12/15/stephen-quake-wins-pioneers-prize/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |language=en-US}}</ref> He was named a [[Clarivate Citation Laureates|Clarivate Citation Laureate]] in Physics (2022).<ref name=":7" />

== Entrepreneurship ==
Quake has been active in translating laboratory innovations into widely used tools and diagnostics through a series of biotechnology companies. Early in his career, he founded [[Standard BioTools|Fluidigm]] (now Standard BioTools) to commercialize the '''integrated microfluidic circuits''' developed in his lab.<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Standard BioTools |url=https://standardbio.com/about/about-us/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Standard BioTools |language=en-US}}</ref> Based on his lab's work on single-molecule sequencing, he founded [[Helicos Biosciences]], which created the first commercial single-molecule [[DNA sequencer]]; Quake used this platform to sequence and publish his own genome as one of the first handful of human genomes available.<ref>{{Cite web |last=page |first=Emily Singerarchive |title=Sequencing a Single Molecule of DNA |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2008/06/23/219906/sequencing-a-single-molecule-of-dna/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=MIT Technology Review |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pushkarev |first1=Dmitry |last2=Neff |first2=Norma F. |last3=Quake |first3=Stephen R. |date=August 2009 |title=Single-molecule sequencing of an individual human genome |journal=Nature Biotechnology |language=en |volume=27 |issue=9 |pages=847–850 |doi=10.1038/nbt.1561 |pmid=19668243 |pmc=4117198 |bibcode=2009NatBi..27..847P |issn=1546-1696}}</ref> After his lab demonstrated the first [[Noninvasive prenatal testing|NIPT]] approach, he co-founded Verinata Health, which was later acquired by Illumina.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Illumina Strengthens Leadership Position in Reproductive Health with Agreement to Acquire Verinata Health, Inc. |url=https://investor.illumina.com/news/press-release-details/2013/Illumina-Strengthens-Leadership-Position-in-Reproductive-Health-withAgreement-to-Acquire-Verinata-Health-Inc/default.aspx |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=investor.illumina.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Work from his group on transplant diagnostics helped found a business later acquired by CareDx in order to launch their cell-free DNA test.<ref>{{Cite press release |last=CareDx |first=CareDx |date=2014-05-22 |title=CareDx Enters Into Agreement to Acquire ImmuMetrix |url=https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2014/05/22/638458/31386/en/CareDx-Enters-Into-Agreement-to-Acquire-ImmuMetrix.html |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=GlobeNewswire News Room |language=en-us}}</ref> More recently, he co-founded Karius to bring '''noninvasive infectious disease tests''' into the clinic.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Advanced Infectious Disease Diagnostics {{!}} Karius |url=https://kariusdx.com/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=kariusdx.com |language=en-US}}</ref> His interests in single-cell biology also led to startups such as Quanticel Pharmaceuticals (acquired by [[Celgene]]) and Cellular Research (acquired by [[BD (company)|Becton, Dickinson and Company]]).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Garde |first=Damian |date=2015-04-27 |title=Celgene to Acquire Quanticel Pharmaceuticals {{!}} Fierce Biotech |url=https://www.fiercebiotech.com/biotech/celgene-to-acquire-quanticel-pharmaceuticals |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.fiercebiotech.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-08-25 |title=BD to Acquire Cellular Research to Develop a Leading Genomics Platform for Single Cell Analysis |url=https://investors.bd.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/491/bd-to-acquire-cellular-research-to-develop-a-leading-genomics-platform-for-single-cell-analysis |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Becton, Dickinson and Company |language=en}}</ref>
